finding.question: Under current U.S. election rules, can a valid domestic mail-in ballot postmarked before Election Day be counted if it arrives afterward, and how does this vary by jurisdiction and arrival date?
finding.summary: Yes. For the November 3, 2020 general election, California required ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if received no later than 17 days afterward, November 20. Oregon, by contrast, required ballots to be received by 8 p.m. on November 3; a postmark did not extend that deadline. North Carolina allowed ballots postmarked by Election Day to arrive by 5 p.m. November 12; on October 28, the U.S. Supreme Court left that extension in place.

report_raw.claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
report_raw.justification: For the November 3, 2020 general election, California required officials to count otherwise valid ballots postmarked on or before Election Day and received within 17 days afterward. [S1] North Carolina also allowed post-Election receipt: its election board proposed a November 12 deadline for ballots postmarked by Election Day, and the Supreme Court left the extension in place. [S3][S4] Rules varied by state: Oregon required ballots to be received by 8 p.m. on Election Day, regardless of postmark. [S2] Inference: A ballot postmarked before Election Day and arriving afterward would not necessarily be thrown out, contrary to the claim.
key_points: California accepted qualifying ballots received up to 17 days after Election Day. [S1]
North Carolina's extended deadline was left in place as of October 28, 2020. [S3][S4]
Oregon required receipt by Election Day and did not count postmarks as meeting its deadline. [S2]
report_raw.counter_argument: The claim accurately describes Oregon's 2020 deadline: a postmark did not extend the time for receipt. [S2] But it does not identify a jurisdiction, and California's rule provides a direct counterexample to a general assertion that all such ballots would be thrown out. [S1]
evidence_gaps: The evidence gives examples rather than an exhaustive inventory of every jurisdiction's 2020 rules.
No jurisdiction or election year was specified in the claim; the cited rules concern the November 2020 general election as of October 28, 2020.
